title: Superpower Glass machine-learning emotion feedback on Google Glass improves socialization scores in children with autism (Stanford cohorts)
summary: Stanford's Superpower Glass cut SRS-2 scores 7.38 points in 14 children and raised Vineland socialization 4.58 points in a 71-child RCT.
account: Superpower Glass, developed at Stanford University, runs a machine-learning facial-expression classifier on Google Glass to show a child which emotion a facing person is displaying. In an at-home feasibility study with intake between July and October 2016 (day not given, so 1 July is used), 14 children with autism completed the protocol; total SRS-2 scores fell an average of 7.38 points and 12 of 14 families reported more eye contact (npj Digital Medicine, 2018). In a randomized trial enrolling 71 children aged 6 to 12 from 1 November 2016 to 11 April 2018, those adding the device to applied behavioral analysis therapy gained 4.58 points more on the Vineland socialization subscale than controls (P = .005), while three other primary measures did not reach significance (JAMA Pediatrics, 2019). Results are cohort-level.
purpose: Teach emotion recognition and facial engagement to children with autism through real-time wearable feedback
system: Superpower Glass: Google Glass with a real-time machine-learning facial emotion classifier and companion smartphone app
developer: Stanford University (Wall lab, Division of Systems Medicine and Department of Computer Science)
deployer: Participating families at home under the Stanford studies
segment: Children with autism spectrum disorder aged 6-12
taxonomy_note: Social-skills learning outcome; Improved Accessibility would also be defensible.

ratings.reason: General benefit without an event: gains are group means (SRS-2 and Vineland) with no individually attributed outcome in the fetched texts.
General benefit without an event: trial evidence of efficacy comparable to standard care, not a measured societal change.

ai_role.statement: The emotion classifier, trained on public facial-expression databases and tuned for home conditions, generates the real-time cues the intervention relies on; the Guess the Emotion game within the package does not use the classifier, so part of the effect may come from structured family interaction rather than the AI.

paired_incident.basis: Both depend on a real-time facial emotion classifier labeling expressions for a user; Face++ and Microsoft's emotion models misread faces systematically, scoring Black people's smiling or ambiguous photos as negative.
